name: VOYAGER
summary: A 3.66 m dish, a ten-sided bus of electronics and three nuclear generators on a boom, trailing a 13 m magnetometer. Launched 1977, still transmitting from interstellar space on about 200 watts.

rooms.name: High-Gain Antenna
rooms.description: A 3.66 m parabolic dish that has to point within a quarter of a degree of Earth or the link drops. It carries the X-band downlink the mission lives on: 115 kbit/s at Jupiter, 160 bit/s from interstellar space, received by 70 m antennas on the ground after a round trip of more than a day and a half.

rooms.name: Spacecraft Bus
rooms.description: A ten-sided ring of electronics bays around the propellant tank: three computers in pairs, the attitude system, and 70 kB of tape recorder that stored images for later playback. Every command since 1977 has been read by the same flight data system, reprogrammed from Earth as instruments and memory failed.

rooms.name: Scan Platform
rooms.description: Two cameras, an infrared spectrometer and an ultraviolet spectrometer on a platform that steers in two axes at the end of a 2.5 m boom, held clear of the bus so it can point independently of the antenna. It is the reason Voyager returned pictures instead of only fields and particles.

rooms.name: Radioisotope Generators
rooms.description: Three generators on their own boom, each with 24 plutonium-238 spheres making heat that thermocouples turn into electricity. Together they gave 470 W at launch and fall about 4 W a year; the mission plans instrument shutdowns against that curve. The boom holds them away from the instruments that would otherwise count their neutrons.

rooms.name: Magnetometer Boom
rooms.description: Thirteen metres of fibreglass boom, stowed in a 0.7 m canister and unfurled after launch, carrying two magnetometers far enough from the spacecraft to read the interplanetary field. It was these instruments that registered the drop in solar-wind particles and the jump in field strength that marked the heliopause.

rooms.name: Golden Record
rooms.description: A gold-plated copper phonograph record bolted to the bus, with a cartridge and a needle, carrying 115 images, greetings in 55 languages, 90 minutes of music and the sounds of a planet. Its aluminium cover is engraved with instructions for playing it and a pulsar map giving the Sun's position. Shelf life: about a billion years.

systems.name: Power
systems.description: Three generators on one bus, shedding instruments as the output falls.

systems.name: Data
systems.description: Instruments to the tape recorder, recorder to the dish, and a day and a half of light-time to Earth.

segments.name: Cruise Configuration
segments.caption: Sixteen metres, no crew, two hundred watts, and forty-eight years of continuous operation.

segments.name: Generators
segments.caption: Three nuclear generators losing four watts a year, which is the mission's real clock.

segments.name: Scan Platform
segments.caption: Two cameras and two spectrometers on a steerable platform, held clear of the bus.

segments.name: Antenna
segments.caption: Three and a half metres of dish that must stay pointed within a quarter of a degree of Earth.

segments.name: Bus
segments.caption: Ten bays of electronics and seventy kilobytes of tape, reprogrammed from Earth for half a century.

segments.name: Golden Record
segments.caption: A hundred and fifteen images, fifty-five languages, and instructions engraved on the cover.

segments.name: Magnetometer
segments.caption: Thirteen metres of boom that measured the field change at the edge of the heliosphere.
